Are digital natives ready to use GenAI for serious work?
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly diffusing across organisations, yet little is known about how digital natives assess its usefulness for business and entrepreneurship (BEC-PU). Understanding how this cohort evaluates GenAI is crucial for responsible organisational adoption. This study investigates whether GenAI tools are perceived as professionally valuable by techno-creative digital natives through their contribution to techno-creative and entrepreneurial (TC/BE) skills. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), UTAUT2 and Task-Technology Fit (TTF), we adopt a multi-stage design combining an exploratory classroom-based qualitative phase and a survey of Spanish undergraduates in techno-creative degrees. Survey data were analysed using PLS-SEM. Results show that artistic generation and writing assistance GenAI tools are positively related to both techno-creative and business–entrepreneurial skills, while basic management tools relate positively to business–entrepreneurial skills. By contrast, audiovisual production tools show no meaningful relationships in the model, and technical specialisation tools display a negative association with techno-creative skills. None of the GenAI categories shows a significant direct effect on BEC-PU. Instead, perceived business usefulness emerges mainly through TC/BE skill development, with the clearest indirect effects observed for artistic generation and writing assistance tools. These findings suggest that digital natives in techno-creative higher education contexts do not yet perceive GenAI as directly useful for “serious” business-oriented work; rather, they attribute business value to GenAI once it has helped them to build capabilities. The study contributes a “learning-to-business-value” perspective on GenAI adoption and offers implications for training and professionalising strategies that strengthen task-fit, usability and the integration of GenAI into creative and entrepreneurial workflows.

title: Exploring the drivers and barriers of digital twin adoption in Kenya and its implications for manufacturing asset optimisation
abstract: The fourth industrial revolution (I4.0) has accelerated the adoption of digital twin technology (DTT) as a system-level enabler of data-driven manufacturing transformation and intelligent asset management. While the literature increasingly recognises the potential of DTT, empirical research examining their adoption within the broader industrial ecosystem in African manufacturing contexts remains scarce. This study investigates DTT adoption in Kenya’s manufacturing sector by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) to develop a behavioural model situated within a nascent industrial ecosystem. Drawing on survey data collected from 257 senior managers and analysed using PLS-SEM, the study finds that DTT use is primarily influenced by managerial attitudes and perceived behavioural control, underscoring the importance of internal organisational readiness and capability-building over external normative pressures. The results also establish a positive relationship between DTT use and manufacturing asset optimisation, highlighting the ecosystemic value of digital transformation strategies in enhancing operational efficiency, predictive maintenance, and real-time decision-making. By advancing a socio-technical and ecosystem-informed perspective, this study offers a novel contribution to digitalisation scholarship in emerging economies and provides actionable insights for firms and policymakers seeking to embed DTT in system-wide industrial modernisation efforts.

title: A taxonomy of business models for data intermediaries
abstract: Both the rising dominance of large platforms in data markets and the increasing exchange of personal data among organizations within data ecosystems have led to significant asymmetries, as individuals have limited control over data-related decisions and restricted access to the value generated from data use. Scholars have called for data intermediaries to help address these asymmetries, yet little research has examined how their business models function within data ecosystems that facilitate personal data exchange. This study examines the key characteristics and archetypes of data intermediary business models that enable the exchange of personal data. Using Nickerson's taxonomy development method and Al-Debei's V4 business model ontology, the research develops a taxonomy of data intermediary business models in data ecosystems centered on personal data exchange and derives archetypes through hierarchical clustering. The identified taxonomy dimensions clarify how these business models operate and create value within personal data ecosystems from a network-level business model perspective. Based on this framework, eight archetypes are identified, illustrating how data intermediaries prioritize interests of different ecosystem actors.

title: The chat dilemma: Usefulness, risk, ethics, and student intentions to use generative AI in higher education
abstract: Academic integrity has been a salient challenge in higher education since the early emergence of generative AI tools and remains a pressing issue as students and institutions continue to negotiate norms for their ethical academic use. This study tested an AI-adapted educational TAM framework with ethical and learning-risk extensions among early student users of ChatGPT. A total of 500 Croatian university students completed a selfreport questionnaire assessing Ease and Reliability of Use, Learning Usefulness and Engagement, Perceived Learning Risks, Ethical Concerns, and Intention to Use ChatGPT for Homework Assignments. MANCOVA revealed significant differences across user profiles. Homework Users reported more favorable evaluations, including higher ease and reliability, learning usefulness and engagement, and intention to use, together with lower perceived risks and ethical concerns. Parallel mediation analyses showed that Learning Usefulness and Engagement was the strongest indirect pathway linking Ease and Reliability of Use with Intention to Use ChatGPT, whereas Ethical Concerns showed a smaller but significant indirect association. Indirect pathways involving Perceived Learning Risks were comparatively weak. Exploratory serial mediation analyses supported a similar pattern, in which higher perceived ease and reliability was associated with greater learning usefulness and engagement, lower ethical concerns, and stronger intentions to use ChatGPT for homework. Overall, the findings suggest that functional, ethical, and risk-related evaluations of generative AI tools are closely associated with students’ intentions toward academic AI use. The study underscores the need for clear institutional guidelines, AI literacy initiatives, and open discussion of responsible AI use in higher education.

title: Tracing moral value drift across large language model generations and their societal implications
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous revision, yet how their moral response tendencies evolve across released editions remains poorly characterized. We present a structured empirical study employing a psychometrically grounded 107-probe instrument covering various moral foundations (e.g., Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity) through adapted questionnaire items, ethical dilemma scenarios, value-priority rankings, and meta-ethical probes, administered uniformly across 14 commercial LLMs spanning 2022–2025 from two providers (OpenAI and Anthropic). We introduce the moral drift analysis (MDA), wherein moral drift denotes measurable temporal change in model-expressed value configurations across successive releases, following the established technical usage of drift in machine learning (e.g., data drift) without implying moral degradation or improvement, as a framework that decomposes value change into stance drift and refusal-policy drift. In total, approximately 9,500 model calls reveal a 14-fold asymmetry in mean moral drift between providers: OpenAI models exhibited substantial mean stance drift (Cohen's d = 0.35, exceeding the conventional small-effect threshold of 0.2), characterized by non-monotonic reversal patterns across generations, while Anthropic models maintained temporal stability. Notably, this provider asymmetry was domain-specific, with moral foundation items driving the overall pattern, while ethical dilemma and value priority probes showed mixed or reversed asymmetries. We discuss implications for alignment stability, value lock-in, and the interpretability of moral response patterns in deployed systems, and release code and instruments to support longitudinal auditing of future model updates.

title: Mediating and moderating mechanisms of the digital bridge between infrastructure and entrepreneurial performance
abstract: Digital infrastructure is widely acknowledged as a critical enabler of entrepreneurial activity; however, empirical evidence explaining how infrastructure translates into superior entrepreneurial performance remains fragmented. This study develops and tests an integrated model explaining the mediating and moderating mechanisms linking digital infrastructure quality to digital entrepreneurial performance. Drawing on the resource-based view, strategic change theory, dynamic capabilities theory, and institutional theory, we conceptualize digital infrastructure as a foundational resource whose performance implications depend on internal capability development, innovation orientation, and regulatory context. Using survey data collected from 300 digital ventures operating in the Middle East, we employ Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) to test direct, mediating, and moderating effects. Results show that digital entrepreneurial capabilities and innovation orientation partially mediate the relationship between infrastructure quality and performance. Innovation orientation emerges as the stronger mediating pathway. Regulatory support significantly moderates five structural relationships, amplifying the performance returns of both infrastructure and internal capabilities. By integrating resource-based, dynamic capability, and institutional perspectives within a single empirical model, the study extends existing research by demonstrating that infrastructure alone is insufficient for high entrepreneurial performance; rather, performance emerges from the interaction between technological readiness, organizational capabilities, innovation culture, and institutional support. The findings offer actionable insights for entrepreneurs and policymakers seeking to convert digital infrastructure investments into sustained competitive advantage.

title: Cultural participation in transition: traditional and emerging forms of culture and the role of smartphones
abstract: Advancements in information technology have reshaped cultural engagement by stimulating emerging cultural practices, such as video games and podcasts, while altering traditional modes of consumption. Smartphones, in particular, are both enablers of cultural participation, providing immediate and continuous access to cultural resources, and a potential distraction that reduces engagement in traditional cultural activities. This study investigates the association between smartphone usage and cultural participation, and is based on a survey conducted in Italy in 2023 (N= 1,220). After identifying five cultural participation profiles, the effect of smartphone usage is investigated through Generalized Propensity Score for continuous treatment, an emerging methodology that can limit confounding biases while controlling for socio-economic and demographic factors. Our findings highlight the existence of cultural participation profiles encompassing both traditional and emerging forms of culture: video games and podcasts. The results, moreover, indicate that the relationship between smartphone usage and cultural participation is not uniform. While the profiles linked to engagement in Popular Cultural Activities, Musical Pursuits and Multimedia Activities benefit from smartphone usage, those relating to participation in Classical and Literary Arts and Performing Arts follow an inverted U-shaped pattern, showing that high or excessive smartphone use ultimately diminishes the user’s engagement in these pursuits.

title: Perceived organized crime risk, R&D investment, and Technical efficiency: Evidence from Italian firms
abstract: This study examines the relationship between perceived organized crime risk and firms’ research and development (R&D) expenditures and technical efficiency. Drawing on a representative sample of more than 2600 Italian firms from the 2020 Bank of Italy Survey, we exploit substantial regional variation in crime risk within a unified national framework. We construct a composite risk indicator using the multi–directional benefit of the doubt methodology and evaluate its association with two central firm dimensions: knowledge investment and productive efficiency. Using instrumental variable (IV) methods for R&D analysis and stochastic frontier analysis and data envelopment analysis for efficiency estimation, we find that higher crime risk is negatively associated with both outcomes. The IV estimates reveal a robust negative relationship with R&D expenditure, while both parametric and nonparametric models indicate a consistent inverse association with technical efficiency. Overall, the findings suggest that greater criminal pressure reduces innovation and weakens firm performance, highlighting the importance of targeted policies aimed at protecting and strengthening local business environments.

title: Building information modelling maturity assessment for industry 5.0 with prescriptive capability pathways
abstract: The construction industry’s digital transformation through Building Information Modelling (BIM) requires a systematic maturity assessment to guide organisational development toward Industry 5.0 (I5.0) principles. Current methods rely heavily on manual evaluation, are exposed to inter-evaluator variability, provide limited computational support, and often overlook the ethical, social and policy implications of technological adoption in emerging economies. This study develops the BIM Maturity Model 5.0 (BMM 5.0), a hybrid computational decision-support framework for BIM maturity assessment. The framework combines Fuzzy Inference Systems for linguistic uncertainty, Shannon Entropy for data-driven criteria weighting, and Elimination Et Choix Traduisant la REalité with n Categories (ELECTRE TRI-nC) for non-compensatory classification across six I5.0-aligned assessment dimensions. BMM 5.0 is demonstrated through a pilot application to eight Brazilian construction projects using the open-source Python tool Maturity Assessment with Fuzzy & Entropy in ELECTRE TRI-nC (MAFE-Tri). Results show that seven projects, representing 87.5% of the sample, reached the C4-Integrated maturity level, while one infrastructure-constrained project was classified as C3-Development, with a maturity score of 28%. These findings suggest that BIM maturity is shaped by organisational, infrastructural and contextual conditions, and should be read as pilot evidence rather than confirmatory validation beyond the studied sample. BMM 5.0 supports on-demand computational assessment under expert oversight, reduces evaluation variability, and generates prescriptive capability-building pathways for sustainable digitalisation. Although empirically applied to construction, its methodological core may be adapted to other domains; however, such transferability requires sector-specific redesign, recalibration and empirical validation. BMM 5.0 connects computational assessment with governance, workforce development and digital inequality concerns, supporting more inclusive and resilient digital transformation.

title: Do intelligent HR technologies spark or stifle employee creativity? A dual-pathway perspective
AI-enabled innovation and firm growth in the Asia–Pacific region: Multilevel and experimental evidence on regulatory climate
Outsider innovation in digital investor communities: How meme coordination reshapes market participation
abstract: This study examines online meme-investing communities as emergent sources of financial innovation. Using a constructivist grounded theory approach to analyze interviews with meme community members and digital trace data, we identify five core dynamics: (1) outsider identity, (2) digital affordances, (3) memetic coordination, (4) distributed learning, and (5) market disruption. Our findings challenge traditional innovation frameworks that prioritize formal institutions by demonstrating how grassroots, digitally coordinated communities can introduce novel financial practices and instruments. Specifically, a shared outsider identity binds community members to a countercultural mission that challenges traditional market norms. Digital platforms enable the rapid dissemination of memetic content, which community members utilize as a coordination device for collective investment decisions. Concurrently, distributed learning processes allow participants to share knowledge and expertise, gradually professionalizing their strategies. These factors together precipitate episodes of market disruption, as seen in recent meme asset rallies that defy conventional valuation logic. The study contributes to innovation theory by introducing the concept of outsider financial innovation, extending user-driven innovation models to financial markets. Practical policy implications include recognizing digitally-mediated investor communities as significant market actors requiring updated regulatory frameworks.

title: Beyond carbon productivity paradox of artificial intelligence through adaptive capability: A perspective of technology complementarity effect
E-Satisfaction and risk perception in government mobile banking applications: A sentiment analysis of user reviews
Cognitive tradeoffs and knowledge mediation in sustained cryptocurrency engagement
Digital financial literacy and entrepreneurial self-efficacy: A balanced scorecard analysis of new venture performance
abstract: Digital finance is now embedded in everyday venturing, yet evidence remains fragmented on whether founders' digital financial literacy (DFL) improves new-venture performance and whether entrepreneurial self-efficacy (ESE) amplifies those gains. Using the complete raw survey (N = 504), we analyze the original DFL (10 items) and ESE (15 items) instruments alongside Balanced Scorecard firm-level outcome indicators (financial, customer, internal, and learning and growth). We estimate standardized moderation models with HC3-robust inference and probe additivity versus synergy through simple-slope and Johnson-Neyman diagnostics. DFL and ESE show sizable, robust associations with financial and customer outcomes, but not with the single-item internal or learning indicators. The principal moderation result is an informative null: the average DFL × ESE interaction is not supported in the mean models. After extending BH-FDR control to exploratory quantile-regression and triple-interaction families, the heterogeneity evidence is retained as hypothesis-generating rather than as a qualification of the main null. Bootstrap mediation analyses with 5,000 resamples suggest that cash flow carries part of the DFL to Financial path and that data analytics provides preliminary evidence for the DFL to Customer path. The evidence supports a bounded, mainly additive account of founder-level digital-finance capability, with causal and domain-general claims limited by the cross-sectional self-report design and single-item BSC outcomes. We derive cautious managerial and policy implications and explain how the UAE context bounds the interpretation of the findings.

title: Middle managers' agency in shaping socially disruptive technologies: Insights into the (re)configuration of human–robot work in Industry 5.0
abstract: This paper investigates how middle managers exercise agency in shaping socially disruptive technologies (SDTs), i.e. technologies capable of transforming established work relations, organisational practices, and normative expectations surrounding work. Within manufacturing, collaborative systems are increasingly introduced as flexible automation solutions that reorganise human–robot work configurations. While existing research has mainly focused on task-level transformations following their deployment, limited attention has been paid to the managerial practices that shape how techno–social disruptiveness unfolds within organisations. Drawing on an interpretive qualitative study based on narrative interviews with 26 middle managers across European manufacturing organisations, this study adopts the combined lenses of the social shaping of technology (SST) and configurational boundary work (CBW) to explore how middle managers act as ‘mediators of disruptiveness’ navigating uncertainty and ethical tensions across four interrelated forms of agency: ‘scouting the potential relevance for collaborative applications’, ‘mobilising alignment within and beyond the organisation’, ‘steering the initial configuration of human–robot work systems’, and ‘unlocking workers’ embodied knowledge’. Our results extend the CBW literature by highlighting middle managers’ agency as a process embedded in multiple temporalities and shaped through the interplay of reflexive and non-reflexive components. The study further problematises the notion of positive compromise in the SST literature and offers an exemplary case account at the organisational level of how SDTs are negotiated and shaped in practice within emerging Industry 5.0 contexts. This perspective gives renewed voice to the role of middle managers, long regarded as ‘ morally muted’ .

title: AI- and robotics-driven reconfiguration of a traditional industry: Business model innovation in agriculture 4.0
abstract: Agriculture 4.0 is introducing digital tools – especially AI and robotics – into farming. More importantly it is transforming one of the world’s most traditional industries, a sector historically anchored in manual labor, tacit knowledge, family-values, product-centric exchange, and deeply sedimented social practices. AI, robotics, connected machinery, and data infrastructures challenge these foundations by shifting agricultural work from human observation, experiential judgment, and field-based execution toward algorithmic monitoring, automated recommendation, and increasingly autonomous operations. Drawing on business model theory, our conceptual study explains how Agriculture 4.0 moves farming from historically embedded, hardware-centered arrangements toward data-driven, service-based, and platform-orchestrated models of value creation, delivery, and capture. We develop an integrative framework and propositions that specify six central transformations: rise of data-driven business models, persistent business model experimentation, strategic realignment through platforms, recurring and outcome-based revenue logics, duality of platform-enabled scaling and platform dependency, and governance challenge of balancing openness with control. By theorizing Agriculture 4.0 as the business model transformation of a traditional industry, our study advances research on digital transformation, platform ecosystems, business model innovation, and sociotechnical disruption. Our framework shows that disruption in traditional sectors requires more than superior technology or economic promise. It gains force only when novel organizational arrangements become accepted as legitimate alternatives to established practices, identities, and sectoral logics.

title: Beyond subsidies: Digital governance, market validation, and the pathway to sustainable development goals-aligned green transformation
Algorithmic transparency and citizen trust in digital governance: A cross-national analysis of AI adoption in public services
Enhancing situation awareness for disaster policymaking via LLM-generated narratives
abstract: Effective disaster policymaking requires accurate situation awareness. Yet, current practices often rely on sparse and fragmented quantitative proxy indicators. This reliance frequently leads to contextual blindness and a loss of the tacit knowledge typically conveyed through narratives. While narrative strategies are known to influence situation awareness, systematically evaluating the impacts of different types of narratives has historically been challenging due to the lack of tools to scalably generate standardized, context-specific narratives. Generative artificial intelligence, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), holds promise for synthesizing fragmented data into standardized, context-rich narratives at scale and low cost. Little is known about the extent to which LLMs can generate different types of narratives and how these narratives influence situation awareness in disaster policymaking. To this end, we introduce a novel methodological framework that utilizes theory-driven prompts to synthesize raw data into distinct narrative styles, i.e., Integral Linkage, Episodic, High Point, and Consequences. We validate this method through a controlled experiment (n=428) set in a simulated Charleston disaster resilience investment scenario. Our results demonstrate that LLMs are effective in generating different types of narratives, while the effects of LLM-generated narratives on decision support are not universal. Integral Linkage narratives significantly improve comprehension and projection by reducing logic errors and enhancing plausibility judgments regarding uncertain information. In contrast, episodic or emotionally charged narratives fail to outperform the raw proxy indicators. Episodic narratives, theorized to facilitate schema building through storytelling, exerted a suppressive mediation effect on situation awareness, while affective mechanisms such as transportation and social identification proved ineffective. These findings clarify when LLM-generated narratives are useful for selected dimensions of policy sensemaking, suggesting that effective policy decision support requires systems designed primarily to amplify analytical processing. This study offers a scalable methodology for policy practitioners to enhance the interpretation of quantitative indicators without losing the nuance of qualitative context.

title: Leveraging generative AI to drive supply chain resilience and sustainable performance: A mediation framework for next-generation supply chains
Does the certification of specialized, refined, characteristic, and innovative (SRCI) enterprises promote breakthroughs in key digital technologies?
Robots and sectoral FDI: Why automation attracts technology-driven but not resource-driven investment in OECD countries
abstract: The rapid diffusion of industrial robots is reshaping global production networks, yet we know surprisingly little about how automation affects the sectoral composition of foreign direct investment (FDI). We argue that robot adoption generates a competitive sorting process among advanced economies—attracting technology-intensive capital through two distinct channels while leaving endowment-driven and site-specific sectors structurally insulated. Using a balanced panel of 32 OECD countries over 2013–2024 and System GMM estimation, we find that robot density significantly increases Manufacturing FDI through a direct productivity channel and Services FDI through an indirect complementarity channel, while Construction, Mining, and Agriculture FDI remain invariant to automation intensity. Strikingly, the complementarity effect on services exceeds the productivity effect on manufacturing in magnitude, suggesting that automation's strongest locational pull operates not where robots are deployed but through cross-sectoral spillovers into knowledge-intensive activities. These findings remain robust to alternative variable measurements. We term this pattern the technological upgrading hypothesis: rather than uniformly reshoring investment from developing countries, automation creates within-OECD differentiation by pulling technology-driven FDI toward automation-frontier economies—a mechanism that aggregate analyses cannot detect and that carries significant implications for the geography of investment and the risk of FDI polarisation among advanced economies.

title: Editorial Board
Building anticipatory capacity for transformative resilience: Lessons from UK and EU applying strategic foresight in grand societal challenge-oriented regional policy
abstract: ABSTRACT Grand Societal Challenges (GSCs) require regional policymakers to develop new forms of anticipatory capacity. This is defined as the ability to navigate uncertainty, align diverse stakeholders and direct development towards long-term societal goals. This study argues that, when implemented throughout the entire policy cycle, strategic foresight is a vital tool for building such capacity and positioning regions for transformative resilience. Using an abductive, qualitative comparative case study design, the research examines three regional foresight processes in the Helsinki-Uusimaa region (Finland), Scotland (UK) and the Basque Country (Spain). The analysis is structured around three integrated dimensions: shared place-based understanding, anticipatory capacity, and reflexivity and monitoring. Rather than introducing new foresight components, the primary contribution lies in the integrated operationalisation of these established dimensions across the full policy cycle within GSC-oriented regional policy contexts. The findings suggest that all three regions use foresight to identify crisis-induced opportunities and align their assets with development priorities driven by challenges. However, their positions differ along the reorientation–transformation continuum. Helsinki-Uusimaa and Scotland primarily demonstrate reorientation, redirecting existing innovation system assets towards new objectives. In contrast, the Basque Country exhibits transformational intent, evidenced by more profound structural reconfiguration. These variations are influenced by pre-existing institutional resources and the specific nature of the GSC addressed. This study helps to bridge the gap between conceptual discussions of transformative innovation and the practical application of foresight in regional policy. It provides policymakers with grounded insights to help them build anticipatory capacity in response to complex, place-specific societal challenges.

title: Critical success factors for GenAI digital products: From technology–market duality to a Technology–Market–Ethics triad
Does digitalization really reduce environmental pressure? Evidence from emerging economies on the digital environmental paradox
abstract: Accelerating digital transformation across emerging economies has sparked intense debate over its net ecological impacts, particularly in fossil-fuel-dependent, energy-intensive production regimes. To clarify this conditional relationship, the environmental effects of digitalization and energy intensity are evaluated across twelve emerging countries (2009–2022) using a distribution-sensitive Method of Moments Quantile Regression (MMQR) framework. Empirical findings confirm the existence of a "digital environmental paradox." While digitalization reduces the overall ecological footprint and delivers stronger mitigation effects in high-environmental-pressure regimes, these benefits systematically weaken as economic energy intensity increases. Energy intensity remains the primary driver of ecological degradation across all quantiles, whereas economic growth follows an Environmental Kuznets Curve pattern with a high turning point. Rather than treating digitalization as a standalone green solution, policymakers must mandate energy-efficient green data centers, link digital infrastructure subsidies directly to renewable energy grids, and implement targeted industrial energy-efficiency retrofits.

title: AI-enabled open innovation: A contingency approach to building organizational resilience
A critical examination of the impact of big data analytics capability on container port performance
abstract: The performance of container ports is increasingly being hampered by port congestion, strict adherence to environmental regulatory frameworks, and inefficiency of border control agencies. Anecdotal evidence indicates that advanced analytics and digitalizing container ports holds much promise to mitigate these challenges. At the same time, a lack of empirical evidence about the effects of big data analytics capability (BDAC) is limiting understanding of how port managers can leverage this novel capability. This study draws on the resource-based view and stakeholder theory to develop and test a model that describes the resources to implement BDAC and subsequently improve four dimensions of port performance (i.e., service quality, operational efficiency, sustainability, and financial performance). We test our research hypotheses using survey data from 175 responses gathered from international container ports that have applied big data analytics. The results support our hypotheses and advance understanding by indicating that BDAC can improve these dimensions of port performance. Specifically, financial performance gains the greatest improvements, whereas operational efficiency gains the least improvements. We provide a comprehensive port assessment framework with four principles and 11 associated key performance indicators. This study illuminates the critical role of tangible, intangible, and human resources in establishing BDAC at the port community level. It also enhances knowledge for port authorities, terminal operators, and other public or private stakeholders of container ports.

title: Generative AI and the uneven disruption of freelance labor: Exposure, diffusion, and adaptation under constraint
Prioritizing Industry 4.0 obstacles for the transition towards Industry 5.0
The impact of digital innovation, geopolitical risk, and oil prices on food production sustainability
Measuring voluntary standards diffusion: A five-step automated web-based framework
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior studies on voluntary standards have employed different methods of measuring diffusion but have yet to develop a multimethod automated framework to methodologically examine the uptake of these voluntary standards at a global scale. Understanding the need for a combined approach, our work provides a five-step automated framework that integrates Web Crawling, Natural Language Processing and Social Network Analysis to measure voluntary standards diffusion across unstructured web data at large scale. In this approach, web crawling is used to extract data from unstructured data sources, Natural Language Processing is used to semantically analyse unstructured information into structured information, and network analysis is used to visualise bipartite and one-mode co-occurrence networks. We present a case study based on the diffusion of the UK 2018 Code of Practice for Consumer IoT Security, to demonstrate how the empirical results from this approach can evaluate voluntary standard initiatives and inform technology governance strategies.

title: The role of technology and exports in shaping skill- and gender-differentiated employment in global value chains
Multidimensional network community structures and breakthrough technology diffusion: Evidence from the AI chip industry
Designing algorithms to manage deep uncertainty in infrastructure projects: The role of psychological artificial intelligence
abstract: Decision-makers in infrastructure projects routinely rely on informal heuristics to navigate volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous conditions. These heuristics are often treated as liabilities, attributed to cognitive bias. However, emerging evidence indicates that when heuristics are deliberately designed, they can match—or even outperform—machine learning models in inference tasks under deep uncertainty. Despite this, systematic algorithms for managing uncertainty associated with delivery-stage events, such as rework, remain underdeveloped. Psychological artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising foundation by focusing on designing efficient, transparent decision rules grounded in human cognition. Against this backdrop, our paper addresses the question: How can psychological AI be used to design and implement algorithms that support the management of rework-related uncertainty? Using an interpretive case study, the analysis examines how experiences within a water infrastructure alliance shaped behavioral processes, specifically recency (memory) and imitation (learning), among personnel involved in a transport mega-project. We reveal that these processes were associated with the enactment of informal decision rules for responding to rework as it emerged. Although psychological AI offers strong potential to generate ecologically rational and transparent decision tools, its application in infrastructure delivery remains limited, and more broadly, in project environments. This paper responds by opening a new line of inquiry into how such tools can be developed to address rework and other unforeseen events. Two contributions are advanced. First, a theoretical framing is introduced to inform the design of simple, interpretable decision algorithms suited to unexpected events in large-scale infrastructure projects. Second, the analysis suggests how psychological principles can be translated into decision rules to guide decision-making under uncertainty.

title: Equal access, unequal gains: How digital capability deficits shape the productivity effects of open government data
AI-driven supply chain innovation: The roles of supply chain ambidexterity and complexity
Silencing controversial realities through prompt revision: The erasure of intensive livestock farming in text-to-image generative AI
abstract: Generative AI like ChatGPT is increasingly integrated into people’s daily lives as a vehicle for information access and to aid decision-making. However, misinformation and biases are embedded in these models, raising ethical concerns. Previous research has revealed AI biases regarding human attributes like skin tone, gender, and geo-culture. To mitigate these biases in text-to-image generative AI models, companies like OpenAI introduced prompt revision, an implicit process of rewriting user prompts to add more details such as showing humans with different genders and skin tones; thereby, promoting diversity. However, rewriting user prompts risks introducing other biases and changing user intention without the user knowing. Using intensive livestock farming as an example, we provide the first evidence that OpenAI’s text-to-image model (DALL-E 3) erased the reality of controversial topics through prompt revision. DALL-E 3 introduces a strong bias toward romanticizing livestock farming, depicting dairy cows grazing on pasture and pigs rooting in mud. This bias remained when we requested realistic depictions. The generated images are in stark contrast to reality where many farmed animals in industrialized countries are reared indoors with limited space per animal, conditions that fail to resonate with societal values. Inhibiting prompt revision resulted in images that more closely reflected modern practices of housing farmed animals indoors; for example, cows were shown feeding through metal headlocks, and pigs were shown behind metal railings on concrete floors. Prompts requesting images of farms in North America, Europe and Oceania yielded mostly pastoral scenes regardless of region, but once prompt-revision was disabled, regional variations emerged. The proportion of outdoor versus indoor housing systems depicted in AI-generated images after prompt-revision was disabled partially reflects actual housing statistics from these regions. Romanticizing and concealing the reality of livestock farming through prompt revision risks reinforcing mis- and disinformation about how farm animals are raised. This disconnect could hinder meaningful dialogue in aligning farming practices with public values, harming the social sustainability of both AI development and livestock farming. Moreover, our study reveals how prompt revision could systematically promote misinformation while silencing the reality. We caution against the broad sweeping romanticization of AI-generated imagery.

title: How demography shapes the macroeconomic returns to automation
abstract: This paper investigates how demographic change interacts with automation to shape long-term macroeconomic outcomes. Using a calibrated general equilibrium model with heterogeneous labor and capital, we simulate five OECD countries with diverse demographic and technological profiles: Republic of Korea, Australia, Italy, Hungary, and Türkiye. Our model replicates key findings from the literature, including the positive relationship between aging and robot accumulation, as well as the growing capital income share at the expense of the labor income share. Beyond these, we uncover several novel insights. First, robot accumulation is driven more by the share of high-skilled labor and production technology than by declining interest rates. Second, while aging initially boosts robotization, this growth is ultimately constrained by the shrinking pool of high-income contributors. Third, only countries with low initial consumption and production relying on low-skilled labor avoid declines in per capita income. Fourth, robotization often replaces rather than expands capital. Fifth, wage convergence between high- and low-skilled workers emerges as a consequence of automation. Finally, increasing general educational attainment does not necessarily raise per capita GDP growth in aging societies undergoing automation. These findings highlight the importance of labor market structure and technological composition in mediating the macroeconomic effects of automation during demographic transitions.

title: Governance-driven agility and innovation in metaverse adoption: Evidence from Pakistan's frontier economy
Breaking out of the straitjacket: Facilitating digital innovation in resource-constrained high-reliability organizations
abstract: This paper addresses digital innovation challenges and facilitation strategies in resource-constrained high-reliability organizations. While the extant literature offers rich insights into the barriers, enablers, and outcomes of digitalization processes, our understanding of how digital innovation occurs in environments characterized by multiple constraints is still limited. Specifically, high-reliability organizations prioritizing reliability of their operations can face significant challenges in their digitalization efforts, which can be further exacerbated by a lack of resources and digital capabilities. Building on two cases of digital innovation in the Swedish urban water and sewerage sector, the paper contributes to the literature by discussing how collaboration between the highly constrained organizations and technology providers can still lead to digitalization against the odds. Specifically, the paper puts forth a multi-level framework capturing digital innovation adoption barriers and facilitation strategies employed by technology providers, and discusses the study’s implications for theory and practice.

title: Medical robotics beyond automation: Human-robot collaboration and the RONNA system as a socio-technical case study
How NFT transaction networks structure digital market participation: Ecosystem-level evidence from Ethereum and Polygon
Can large language models detect green leaders? CEO environmental backgrounds and corporate ESG performance
Navigating the DEIverse: A comprehensive review and research agenda on diversity, equity, and inclusion in the metaverse
abstract: ABSTRACT Metaverse platforms are shifting from speculative visions to deployed infrastructures and intensifying diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) concerns through embodied participation, intensive data capture, and platform governance. We use the DEIverse as a cartographic label for the research space where metaverse technologies intersect with DEI concerns and map its topic structure. We compile 176 publications (2007-2024) from Scopus, Web of Science, and curated Google Scholar records and combine bibliometric science mapping based on co-word analysis with theory-informed content analysis. We identify ten topics that cluster as motor (“Learning”, “Ethics”, “Healthcare”), niche (“Regulation”, “Autism”), emerging (“Blockchain”, “Safety”, “Accessibility”), and transversal (“COVID-19”, “Avatar”). We interpret the clusters through critical race theory, intersectionality, disability studies, and critical data studies and distill three claims and nine propositions. Layered access divides make connectivity, affordability, embodied usability, and institutional e-capacity key participation thresholds. Datafied embodiment converts behavioral and biometric capture into profiling, surveillance, and classification pressures that reshape privacy, autonomy, and due process. Governance and valuation regimes distribute voice, safety, and opportunity through identity rules, moderation architectures, standards, and virtual asset infrastructures. The integrative matrix situates these propositions across micro, meso, and macro levels and reveals a dual-track field: application-oriented work in education and health outpaces structural analyses of accessibility, labor, and global asymmetries. We conclude with a multilevel research agenda for measuring distributional effects, strengthening data governance and redress, and designing inclusive immersive infrastructures.

title: Reconfiguring the global factory: The synergistic role of additive manufacturing, explainable AI, and knowledge acquisition in MNC operations
Knowledge democratization or cognition homogenization? The double-edged role of generative AI in breakthrough product innovation
Divergent effects of innovation on income inequality: An input-based approach
Information and communication technology as an enabler for circular manufacturing systems: A simulation-based case study in the automotive aftermarket sector
abstract: Circular Manufacturing Systems (CMS) offer a promising pathway toward sustainable production but face implementation challenges, particularly regarding the availability, accessibility, and reliability of information flow across the entire value chain. This study investigates the role of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) as a key enabler of CMS and quantifies its impact on CMS performance. A multi-method simulation modeling approach, integrating agent-based and discrete-event methods, is applied to a case study in the automotive aftermarket sector. Results show that enhanced information transparency and accessibility in the case study's value chain increase remanufacturing by 5% and decrease financial losses for wholesalers by 7-8%. The findings also reveal a shift in the redistribution of returned products among remanufacturers, driven by wholesalers' data-driven decisions based on profitability, remanufacturers' acceptance rates, and return window duration. The results analysis shows that when wholesalers have full visibility into these parameters, product return decisions are no longer based solely on the issuer of the right-to-return options but on multiple criteria, enabling more informed decision-making, improved remanufacturing outcomes, and a more competitive remanufacturing ecosystem. By quantifying the value of information and improved transparency in a real-world case study, this study provides empirical evidence on the role of ICT in CMS implementation beyond qualitative and descriptive accounts. It also offers a simulation-based approach for researchers and practitioners to evaluate the impact of enhanced transparency in complex, inter-organizational value chains, particularly where stakeholders differ in their control over the value chain and their commitment to circularity. The findings reinforce the strategic role of ICT not only as a digital support tool but as a systemic enabler and highlight the importance of interoperable data infrastructures and inter-organizational collaboration.

title: Working with AI, wrestling with ethics: How collaboration and ethical anxiety drive employees’ digital-intelligence transformation self-efficacy
Retraction notice to “Digital transformation and social equity: Bridging the gap in post-pandemic societies” [Technology in Society 87 (2026) 103403]
Persuasiveness of virtual news anchors: Unveiling the influence of gestures, speech rate, and attire
Clarifying the association between digital media engagement and risk taking
abstract: In two cross-sectional studies, we examined the association between smartphone and social media use (SSMU) and risk-taking behavior, focusing on the psychological mechanisms and dimensions of media engagement that may underlie this relationship. In Study 1, we tested whether individual differences in impulsivity, reward sensitivity, and exploratory tendencies accounted for associations between SSMU and multiple forms of risk taking, and whether engagement with more socially interactive platforms differentially related to risk behavior. Results showed that risk taking was associated with SSMU above and beyond specific psychological traits. Negative low-stakes risk taking emerged as the strongest and most consistent correlate of SSMU, and this association was stronger for use of more highly socially interactive platforms. In Study 2, these analyses were conceptually replicated in a larger sample spanning adolescent and young adult cohorts. Across developmental stages, risk taking, particularly involving low-stakes negative risks, remained a robust correlate of SSMU, whereas associations with dispositional traits varied by age group. Together, these findings suggest that SSMU is uniquely linked to everyday forms of risk taking in ways that are not fully captured by broader dispositional traits.

title: Unlocking the data bottleneck: How data factor marketization drives the smart-green synergistic transformation of SEIs
Designing and validating an AI-enabled digital platform to foster circular business models
abstract: The European Union's Circular Economy Action Plan recognises digitalization as a key enabler for fostering Circular Business Models (CBMs). This study aims to design an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-integrated digital platform that orchestrates an industrial ecosystem by connecting relevant stakeholders. The proposed platform incorporates structured data flows, resource-matching capabilities, and modular decision-support components to facilitate the development of CBMs. The study adopts a design science research approach, in which the platform is conceptualized as an artefact developed through iterative cycles of relevance, rigour, and design. Furthermore, the platform leverages a k-means clustering-based AI algorithm to identify potential donor-recipient relationships within CBMs, thereby enhancing decision autonomy. This research integrates orchestration theory with AI-enabled decision autonomy to support circular value exchanges within a digital platform ecosystem. The proposed approach is validated through a case study of the Trentino region, using 200 industrial records from the Modello Unico di Dichiarazione Ambientale (MUD) system. The results demonstrate an 88% precision rate in donor-recipient matching, while expert validation indicates a high donor identification capability (approximately 90%) for supporting transition pathway identification. The findings demonstrate strong alignment between the AI functionality and circular resource flows. Overall, the proposed clustering approach enhances ecosystem connectivity across diverse industrial sectors, providing a pathway for the transition from linear to digitally enabled circular business models.

Feeling like I can make the real me: How trans and gender diverse adults use gaming avatars to explore gender in digital gaming
abstract: Trans and gender diverse (TGD) adults experience many challenges when negotiating their gender identities. This study investigates how TGD individuals use customizable avatars within digital gaming spaces to explore and express gender identities, underscoring the significance of avatar customization for identity affirmation and the influence of online gaming experiences on broader gender presentation. Participants included 79 TGD adults aged 18-37 (M = 24.71 years, SD = 3.78 years) engaging in digital gaming. An online survey presented questions regarding avatar customisation, game limitations, interpersonal role playing, and perceived impacts in other contexts. Broadly, customisation was associated with increased enjoyment, empowerment, and authentic self-representation, while restricted customisation reduced engagement, potentially triggering distress or dysphoria. Participants also highlighted challenges related to the impact of game restrictions on avatar customization. Identity exploration was important for pre-transition exploration and ongoing experimentation, reiterating the importance of authentic connection between avatars and the identified self. Participants reported varied experiences with interpersonal role-playing, with some respondents being avoidant due to anxiety or gender-based harassment, while others reported positive experiences and social connection. Broader impacts included support for coming out, increased confidence in gender expression, and creation of communities. Game designer recommendations include offering diverse avatar customization options and creating androgynous and diverse traits to enhance gaming experiences for TGD players.

title: Governing digital innovation ecosystems under risk and uncertainty: IP circulation, platform dependency, and policy orchestration in Korean content industries
abstract: Digital innovation in cultural and creative industries unfolds under compounded risk and uncertainty, where, drawing on Knight’s (1921) distinction, firms face both calculable ”known unknowns” of platform competition, production cost volatility, and shifting audience attention, and structurally indeterminate ”unknown unknowns” generated by generative AI, platform restructuring, and contested intellectual property (IP) appropriation. Existing innovation ecosystem theories, grounded largely in manufacturing and technology-driven contexts, struggle to explain how value creation, coordination, and governance operate in industries centered on intangible and symbolic assets under platform dependency. Addressing this gap, this study develops a conceptual framework for digital innovation ecosystems in content industries under conditions of high risk and high uncertainty. Methodologically, it employs a qualitative, mechanism-oriented theory-building design combining integrative literature synthesis with abductive interpretive analysis of policy, institutional, and industry materials. The framework is empirically illustrated through the Korean content industry between 2023 and 2026, where IP, digital platforms, and policy institutions interact under intense platform dependency and AI-driven transformation. The study reconceptualizes content innovation ecosystems as systems structured around IP, coordinated through digital platforms, and aligned through policy orchestration, identifying three interdependent mechanisms: IP circulation, platform coordination, and network integration. The study extends innovation ecosystem theory and contributes to debates on managing unknowns in digital innovation.

title: Before imperfections escalate: How inoculation warnings by service robots shape customer responses to minor service imperfections
Do government R&D subsidies promote or constrain disruptive innovation in early-stage ventures? The moderating role of appropriation mechanisms
abstract: Governments promote R&D support as a lever for innovation, yet the evidence on whether such support yields disruptive innovation is unsettled. Prior work has explained the effects of public R&D support largely through financial additionality and signalling, which tells us little about how state support shapes the technological paths firms actually pursue. We draw on institutional theory to argue that government R&D support raises disruptive innovation by increasing technology transfer intensity, which exposes firms to varied knowledge sources and to technological alternatives they would not otherwise encounter. Whether that exposure pays off, however, depends on how firms reconcile openness with value capture. We therefore expect formal appropriation mechanisms to weaken, and informal mechanisms to strengthen, the link between technology transfer intensity and disruptive innovation. Two-wave, multi-informant data from 313 new ventures in Vietnam support these arguments. By specifying both the mechanism and its boundary conditions, the study advances research on disruptive innovation, public innovation policy and appropriation strategy.

title: Understanding generative AI effects on sustainable consumption outcomes: A complementary analytical approach
Voices that connect: Exploring human-like attributes and eWOM in AI assistants
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered voice assistants rely on users’ electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) to support their diffusion and ongoing improvement, yet little is known about which human-like attributes users are most likely to share with others. To address this gap, we employ a sequential mixed-methods design. Study 1 combines topic modeling with qualitative thematic analysis of posts from an online user community and identifies five attributes: general intelligence, personalized responses, human-like cues, warmth, and empathy. In Study 2, survey data from 334 voice assistant users are analyzed to test a media naturalness model linking these attributes to eWOM. Results show that all five attributes are positively associated with eWOM through automated social presence and user engagement. Automated social presence fully mediates the association between human-like cues and eWOM, while partly mediating the relationship for the other four attributes. By integrating machine-learning, qualitative, and survey-based methods, the research advances understanding of human-AI communication and provides insights for designing and managing voice assistant experiences that encourage positive eWOM.

title: High-technology manufacturing and environment nexus: Insights from Spanish manufacturing titans
Specification cost: Relocating the binding constraint in delegation to AI agents with externally supplied objectives
abstract: Firms and investors now delegate consequential financial decisions to artificial intelligence (AI) agents that pursue a specified objective and hold no motivation of their own. Agency theory, the standard account of delegation, treats the loss from delegation as a product of the agent’s divergent motivation, and it disciplines that motivation through monitoring and incentives. Stewardship theory treats the agent’s motivation as already aligned and expects no such loss. Such an agent fits neither case because it has no independently held objective, and delegation to it still results in patterned and costly failure. The argument covers AI systems governed by externally supplied objectives, and the deployed agent system is the unit of analysis. We argue that the binding constraint in this setting is the contractibility of the principal’s objective rather than the agent’s motivation, and we relocate the central friction accordingly. We define specification cost as the delegation loss that remains once interest divergence is removed, the loss that arises because the principal cannot fully specify what the agent should do. The construct is distinct from agency cost, whose incentive component falls to zero when motivation aligns. We state predictions that agency theory and incomplete-contracting theory do not ordinarily derive for populations of machine agents. Specification cost rises with the novelty of the deployment environment; it correlates across agents that share training, producing systemic rather than diversifiable failure; and it can increase when performance-contingent grants expand the agent’s discretionary control over transferable resources. We develop these as testable propositions, ground them in documented cases, and set an agenda for finance and forecasting.

title: AI technology threat perception and occupational anxiety: The dual buffering role of skill adaptability and industry support
abstract: ABSTRACT Based on Conservation of Resources theory and Cognitive Appraisal Theory, this study explored how AI technology threat perception affects occupational anxiety among 387 creative industry professionals, focusing on the dual roles of skill adaptability and industry support. An integrative theoretical model encompassing mediating and moderating mechanisms was constructed and empirically tested. Results indicate that skill adaptability plays a dual role. It mediates the relationship between AI technology threat perception and occupational anxiety, where threat perception indirectly increases anxiety by weakening adaptability. It also positively moderates this relationship, causing highly adaptable individuals to exhibit stronger anxiety when facing AI threats. Meanwhile, industry support exhibits a resource paradox. It directly predicts higher anxiety levels but negatively moderates the threat-anxiety relationship under high threat conditions, acting as a buffer. The empirical testing of this theoretical model reveals that skill adaptability, as a key psychological resource, is complex, and support can sometimes be counterproductive. This enriches the traditional Conservation of Resources theory and provides actionable empirical evidence for future research on complex individual and conditional resources, as well as for implementing differentiated intervention strategies.

title: Virtual collective consciousness in metaverse communities: Sociological insights from collective effervescence and networked sociality
Exploring technology acceptance of ChatGPT consumers: A combined TAM-SOR framework on perceived fee and consumer innovativeness
abstract: As a significant milestone in the rapid developments in artificial intelligence, Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools provide their consumers a wide range of services, including information generation, content generation, learning, and decision-making. Therefore, consumer behavior towards these new tools is becoming increasingly critical. However, the number of studies examining consumer acceptance of Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer (ChatGPT), a prominent tool in the market, is quite limited. This study empirically examines ChatGPT usage and acceptance behavior within the framework of perceived fee and consumer innovativeness, drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) models. Surveys obtained from 231 ChatGPT consumers in Türkiye were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling in SmartPLS. The findings reveal that perceived fee significantly influences consumers' perceptions of value and ease of use as a stimulus. Similarly, consumer innovativeness also shapes perceived value, enjoyment, ease of use, and usefulness, all of which play a central role in consumers' cognitive and affective processes. Finally, perceived value, ease of use, and usefulness are key determinants that guide consumers' purchase decisions. By combining the SOR and the TAM frameworks, this study provides a unique integrated conceptual model of the behavioral processes of GenAI consumers, contributing both theoretically to the literature and practical implications for the GenAI market for improvements in some capabilities such as interface design, guidance, and speed.

title: Affordance entrenchment analysis: A diagnostic tool for technology foresight
abstract: Technological artefacts can acquire new functions without undergoing change in their physical properties. Existing futures methods provide limited analytical purchase on these kinds of transformations, because they generally lack mechanisms for explaining how artefacts acquire new functions through changing practice. This paper introduces affordance entrenchment analysis (AEA), a diagnostic tool designed for use by forecasting professionals, anticipatory governance practitioners, and analysts in technology assessment or research investment roles. AEA directs analytical attention toward three factors that conventional approaches tend to overlook: (1) latent affordances (those capabilities grounded in an artefact's physical properties that no current domain of practice exploits), which circumscribe the possibility space for function change; (2) the formation of structured domains of practice, which determine which of those capabilities become valued; and (3) the consolidation of use (via infrastructure and institutional recognition) through which novel functions take hold. The tool is grounded in Nelson Goodman's work on exemplification and symbol systems and is operationalised through three orienting questions with associated empirical indicators. Applied to a given artefact, AEA structures an assessment of where function change may be occurring and how far it has progressed. This assessment can feed the driving-force identification stage of scenario planning exercises. The paper illustrates the tool through a retrospective case study of Nvidia's graphics processing units and a prospective sketch applying AEA to large language models.

Communicating servitisation offers for mitigating weather-related risk for the construction industry through a simulation based serious game
abstract: Climate change is a pressing global challenge that significantly impacts the day-to-day operations of various sectors, including the construction industry. The construction sector, in particular, experiences severe consequences due to the unpredictability of weather conditions. This unpredictability poses significant challenges for effective planning, risk management, and obtaining appropriate insurance coverage for construction projects. Servatization is transforming business models across many sectors, including the financial sector, where parametric insurance products are being introduced as Digitally Enhanced Advanced Services (DEAS) to facilitate weather risk management for the construction industry. While these services aredesigned to enhance accuracy and streamline the operations and processes, their complexity often makes them difficult for end users to understand and evaluate. As a result, limited exposure and understanding of servitisation offerings can negatively impact the uptake of the service. This research collaborated with real-life servitisation designers - (EHAB) within the construction industry to capture the key factors impacting the communication and understanding of servitisation offer. Based on these insights, it then designed & developed a prototype simulation based serious game to communicate the servitisation offer to end users. The serious game enables users to experience weather-related risks and the operational logic of parametric insurance through interactive, simulation-based gameplay, allowing long-term impacts to be explored within a short game cycle.Quantitative methods was used to evaluatethe effectiveness of simulation-based serious games, involving 50 participants from the construction sector. The evaluation focused on perceived usefulness, ease of use, engagement, and overall user experience. The results indicate positive user perceptions and suggest that serious games can provide an effective and engaging medium for communicating complex servitisation offerings related to weather risk management in construction.

title: Enabling reuse of construction and demolition waste with data spaces: Potentials and limitations in the transition to circularity
abstract: In 2022, the Architecture, Engineering, Construction, and Operations (AECO) industry generated 39.8 million tons of Construction and Demolition Waste (CDW). Despite the growing interest in circularity, the direct reuse of CDW remains limited due to technical, economic, regulatory, and organizational barriers. A major challenge is the lack of accessible information. Data spaces offer a promising framework to address this issue, but they have not yet been applied to CDW reuse in the AECO industry, leaving their potential to overcome these challenges unclear. This paper assesses the potential of data spaces by identifying practical use cases where they could support CDW reuse, while also highlighting their limitations and the need for complementary societal and institutional actions. Drawing on the multi-level perspective, the study situates technological innovation within the context of a broader socio-technical transition to circularity. A mixed-method approach was adopted, including stakeholder interviews, prototype development, use case identification, and a participatory workshop with industry experts. Findings indicate that data spaces can enhance access to life-cycle information, improve interoperability, and foster trust. However, challenges related to market dynamics, regulatory misalignments, and organisational incentives persist, underscoring the limitations of technology alone. The study concludes that data spaces can contribute to the transition toward circularity but must be embedded within broader socio-technical strategies. Future research should investigate how socio-economic and regulatory challenges can be addressed in conjunction with technological innovation to unlock the full potential of data spaces for the circularity transition.

Toward a multilevel understanding of knowledge hiding in digital workplaces: Insights and opportunities
abstract: This study provides a multilevel synthesis of knowledge hiding (KH) and workplace digital technologies (DTs) literature. While these streams have been examined separately, research at the intersection of KH and workplace DTs remains fragmented. Prior research shows that KH not only occurs at the individual level, but also at the team and organizational levels. Across these same levels, DTs reshape how work is coordinated, how communication unfolds, and how autonomy, interdependence, and control are structured. Together, these developments make a multilevel understanding of KH essential for understanding knowledge dynamics in digital workplaces. To address this need, we conducted a systematic literature review and examined 39 empirical studies. The review identifies key themes, theoretical perspectives, and research gaps across employee, team, and organizational levels. Our findings reveal a strong focus on individual-level antecedents of KH, with limited attention to the team and organizational level. Although DTs are typically implemented to facilitate knowledge sharing, our synthesis shows that they can unintentionally exacerbate KH by creating relational and cognitive strains that unfold across multiple levels. Building on these insights, we propose a multilevel framework to guide future research. This study advances understanding of knowledge dynamics in digital workplaces by highlighting both the enabling and constraining effects of DTs on knowledge exchange. In doing so, it contributes to broader debates on the organizational consequences of digitalization and provides actionable insights for managing knowledge behaviors across organizational levels.

Artificial intelligence and job design: Insights from Job Demands–Resources theory
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming work by reshaping how jobs are designed, experienced, and performed. This article reviews emerging evidence on the implications of AI adoption for job design from the perspective of Job Demands–Resources theory. We develop a conceptual framework that explains how AI adoption may alter the balance between job demands and job resources, and thereby influence both motivational and health-impairment processes. We further propose AI readiness resources (AI-R) – including personal resources, such as AI self-efficacy, and job resources, such as colleague support for AI – as important conditions that help explain when AI adoption is more likely to strengthen rather than undermine employee well-being and performance. Building on this framework, we formulate three guiding principles for future research. First, scholars should distinguish the level of AI adoption, namely top-down versus bottom-up adoption, from the type of AI use, namely automation versus augmentation, because these dimensions may have different job design implications. Second, researchers should differentiate AI-R resources at the personal and job levels, as they point to different mechanisms and intervention opportunities. Third, research should approach AI adoption as a dynamic process in which employee well-being, performance, and AI readiness may influence one another over time. The article concludes with an agenda for future research and practical directions for designing AI-enhanced jobs that are meaningful, motivating, and sustainable.
