Artificial intelligence in academic research: Adoption, productivity, and skill perceptions
abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly expanding across various professional domains, including academia. Yet, limited empirical evidence exists on which academics are adopting AI, how it influences their research productivity, and what implications it holds for their skillsets. Contributing to ongoing debates on the impact of AI on scientific work, this study draws on original data from a recent large-scale survey of Italian academics to explore patterns of AI use, perceived effects on research output, and skill development. Our findings reveal that 39% of respondents report using AI, with significant variation depending on the type of research activity and stage of the research process. AI adoption is more prevalent among younger scholars and those engaged in applied or interdisciplinary research. Overall, AI use is positively associated with higher research productivity and with more favourable expectations about the impact of AI on researchers’ skills. However, the analysis also uncovers nuanced attitudes towards AI: trust in these technologies is not universal, and pockets of scepticism persist across segments of the academic population.

title: Understanding consumer behaviours: A study of ICT expenditure and digital access divide in Spain
abstract: This paper examines the digital access divide in Spain, with a particular focus on the impact of socio-economic factors, territorial disparities and public policies on household investment and access to information and communication technologies (ICT). The analysis, which is based on panel data from the Spanish National Statistics Institute (2016-2022), employs robust econometric models and spatial distributions of expenditure or investment in ICT. This paper presents a particularly interesting context around the digital access divide in Spain. While rural and depopulated areas face significant barriers to full participation in the digital economy, due to lack of infrastructure and an ageing population, coupled with a reluctance to invest in ICT. There is relatively universal access to mobile and internet in Spain.The findings further demonstrate that younger, higher-income individuals are more likely to overcome these barriers, while gender disparities in ICT ownership and investment persist. The study underlines the importance of targeted policies to address the digital divide, particularly through enhanced telecommunications infrastructure and digitalisation efforts by advocating investment in smart infrastructure, digitisation of the workplace, and comprehensive digital skills training, which are essential to foster an inclusive and sustainable digital transformation across all regions.

title: An assessment for trust and misbehavior in Internet of Medical Things (IoMTs) technologies: An improved decision making approach
Green innovation performance assessment in European Countries: A quartile-based decision support framework
How do interdisciplinary pathways shape gender diversity in ICT? Evidence from a quantitative study
abstract: Despite the growing demand for skilled Information and Communication Technology (ICT) professionals and the many initiatives aimed at broadening participation, women remain markedly underrepresented in computer science and related areas. Identifying and assessing educational interventions, including those implemented in higher education, can inform targeted actions to reduce this barrier. By observing the significant impact and extensive intersection of computer science with many other disciplines, in the last few years academic institutions have been expanding their offerings to include a variety of interdisciplinary programs and courses. Recognizing this trend, this paper aims to explore the interest of female students in interdisciplinary topics. Our fundamental question is whether novel programs that cross the boundaries of different disciplines have the potential to attract to ICT more women with respect to traditional programs. To shed light on this issue, we perform a thorough quantitative analysis on extensive data related to students’ enrollment in the whole set of Italian academic programs, both at the bachelor and master level, over many academic years. Our analysis reveals that interdisciplinary programs, such as those blending computer science with domains such as economics, management, finance, and governance, exhibit a substantially higher enrollment of female students (plus 16% on average) than traditional programs. Some specific fields, including artificial intelligence and cybersecurity, benefit even more from interdisciplinarity, with an uplift exceeding 25 percentage points. As a by-product of our study, we also characterize interdisciplinary programs in Italy and quantify students’ propensity across computer-science subdomains, assessing their appeal through a gender lens.

title: From basic actions to subversive affordances: Development and validation of the social media algorithmic resistance scale (SM-ARS)
abstract: As social media platforms increasingly govern civic visibility and information access through opaque, NLP-driven algorithms, the power dynamic between users and technological infrastructures has become highly asymmetric. In response, user behavior has evolved from episodic platform rejection to complex, continuous practices of everyday digital resistance. However, existing research relies heavily on binary models of adoption versus discontinuance and lacks empirical instruments to capture how users reclaim agency post-adoption. To address this gap, this paper conceptualizes, develops, and validates the Social Media Algorithmic Resistance Scale (SM-ARS). Following a rigorous scale development paradigm, an exploratory phase (Study 1: N = 303) identified a multidimensional structure comprising three distinct behavioral repertoires: avoidant resistance (AR), which involves limiting structural exposure; obfuscatory resistance (OR), which involves strategic data pollution to subvert profiling; and counter-curative resistance (CCR), which involves redirected algorithmic curation and algorithmic contestation. A subsequent confirmatory phase (Study 2: N = 611) validated this structure, demonstrating strong model fit and nomological validity through significant associations with algorithm awareness and perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR). Theoretically, the SM-ARS innovates affordance theory by introducing subversive affordances, demonstrating how respondents may strategically repurpose engagement mechanisms to disrupt platform dataveillance. Practically, this instrument provides an initial diagnostic tool for examining how social media users negotiate algorithmic power and protect their digital autonomy. However, its applicability beyond the Romanian context requires further cross-cultural validation.

title: The role of digital platforms to enable industrial symbiosis: unveiling outcomes, drivers and barriers
abstract: This paper focuses on the intersection of digital platforms and industrial symbiosis, which represents a collaborative circular economy paradigm that brings together actors that exchange resources in mutually beneficial relationships. While scholars have acknowledged that digital platforms are one of the main enablers of circular economy and industrial symbiosis, literature on the role of digital platforms in enabling industrial symbiosis is scarce, and the factors that affect their use remain unclear. Scholars have called for more empirical evidence on this matter, which has been mainly investigated through theoretical and quantitative approaches. In the present paper, we deploy a two-step methodology. First, we review existing literature to identify three typologies of digital platforms as industrial symbiosis enablers; namely, digital platforms per se, those enhanced by artificial intelligence, and those enhanced by blockchain. Second, we conduct an exploratory empirical analysis to characterise their use. As a result, this paper reveals the outcomes generated by the identified typologies of digital platforms, together with the barriers and drivers that need to be overcome or leveraged to promote their use. We note that environmental and economic aspects need to be considered together to promote the use of digital platforms to enable industrial symbiosis. We highlight that managerial commitment is key to support the use of digital platforms. We also provide contrasting evidence on the effectiveness of digital platforms in building trust among the actors implementing industrial symbiosis. Finally, we encourage managers to use digital platforms and consider them as relevant tools to enable industrial symbiosis and improve environmental as well as economic performance.

title: Institutional elasticity, digital niches, and industrial upgrading: A comparative study of Sichuan and Zhejiang's economic development in China
From access to innovation: Curiosity and reflection in the uneven realisation of generative AI's value at work
A methodology for investigating technological changes driven by social events: The case of COVID-19
Whose AI problem? Critical narratives and practitioner problematizations
abstract: ABSTRACT: Public and scholarly debates about Artificial Intelligence (AI) often revolve around recurring problem labels, including opacity, accountability, accuracy, trust, and technical literacy. These labels also appear in organizational settings where AI systems are developed and implemented. However, this apparent overlap may conceal important differences in the meanings, values, and practical consequences attached to these labels. Drawing on two ethnographic case studies of AI implementation in maritime shipping and automotive manufacturing, this article examines the relationship between critical and governance-oriented AI problem narratives and practitioner problematizations. The article argues that this relationship is not best understood as a translation from general debate into local practice, but rather as a partial correspondence in which similar problem labels are used across contexts but attached to different values, forms of evaluation, and suggested solutions. In the cases examined here, accuracy, opacity, trust, literacy, and code access became problems of usability, debugging, certification, reliability, investment value, and organizational responsibility, rather than simply questions of public transparency, democratic accountability, or general AI literacy. This suggests that broad AI concerns do not become relevant in organizational settings merely because familiar problem labels are invoked, but when they can be connected to specific responsibilities, forms of evidence, and possibilities for action. The article contributes to STS and organizational research on AI by showing how critical and governance-oriented AI problem narratives and practitioner problematizations can partially correspond without naming the same problems or implying the same responses.

title: The Thucydides Trap in the age of AI: Automated science, global technological advancement, and the governance of technological acceleration
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into scientific research, governance, and strategic competition is reshaping the foundations of global power. In this context, the “Thucydides Trap” describes a structural dynamic in which the rise of a new power generates fear and strategic tension in an established power, increasing the risk of escalation. While widely used to interpret geopolitical rivalry, its application to the age of AI remains incomplete, as it does not account for the systemic effects of technological acceleration and automated knowledge production. This article examines how AI, automated science, and the prospect of artificial general intelligence (AGI) transform both the dynamics of strategic competition and the capacity for global governance. It argues that contemporary technological rivalry is increasingly structured by three interrelated processes: the emergence of AGI as a capability horizon, the automation of scientific discovery as a mechanism of power, and the growing mismatch between technological acceleration and governance capacity. To capture these dynamics, the article introduces the concept of global technological advancement (GTA) as a system-level process linking accelerated knowledge production, infrastructure concentration, and strategic competition. Rather than treating technological leadership as the primary outcome of rivalry, the analysis identifies the governance of technological acceleration under conditions of opacity, compressed time, and institutional fragmentation as the central challenge. Drawing on an interdisciplinary synthesis of international relations, science and technology studies, AI governance, and AI safety, the article reformulates the Thucydides Trap as a problem not only of power transition, but of governing sociotechnical systems under conditions of rapid and uneven technological change. The central question is therefore not who leads in AI, but whether governance systems can adapt quickly enough to prevent competitive dynamics from transforming technological innovation into a source of systemic instability.

Advanced digital technology adoption under risk and uncertainty: A multi-method study of retail firms
abstract: This study examines how financial, technological and institutional risk, together with market and ecosystem uncertainty, shape advanced digital technology adoption in retail firms. Drawing on the distinction between risk as identifiable adoption barriers and uncertainty as ambiguity about future market and ecosystem conditions, the study analyses firm-level data from 1,256 retail firms in EU Member States. The empirical strategy combines logit and probit models, XGBoost, LightGBM, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). The results show that risk is negatively associated with advanced digital technology adoption, whereas uncertainty is positively associated with adoption. However, the interaction between risk and uncertainty is negative, indicating that identifiable barriers weaken the positive association between uncertainty and adoption. The machine-learning models provide similar predictive performance to the regression models and confirm the relevance of uncertainty, risk, firm size, innovation intensity and contextual conditions. The fsQCA results further show that adoption can occur through multiple configurational pathways involving risk, uncertainty, firm size, finance access, digital growth orientation and ecosystem embeddedness. The study contributes to digital transformation research by showing that uncertainty may stimulate digital adoption, but only when firms have sufficient capacity to respond and risk does not excessively constrain action.

title: Digital technologies as drivers of business model innovation in UAE retail startups
abstract: The present study examines the association between the adoption of three digital technologies, viz., artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, and big data analytics, and business model innovation (BMI) among retail startups in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Building on the resource-based and dynamic capabilities (DC) perspectives, we develop a conceptual framework linking digital technology integration (DTI) to value creation, delivery, and capture. Using survey data from 86 UAE-based retail startups, we find that AI and big data analytics are most strongly associated with perceived BMI, with AI most closely linked to value creation and big data most closely linked to value delivery and value capture; blockchain shows a weaker and more selective association. Strategic partnerships strengthen the association between AI adoption and BMI, and organizational capabilities (technical capability and financial resources) partially mediate the relationship between digital technology adoption and BMI. Because the design is cross-sectional and self-reported, these findings should be interpreted as perceived associations rather than causal effects. The study offers practical and policy-relevant insights for startups, policymakers, and other stakeholders navigating digital technology adoption in a digitally ambitious emerging-market economy, and it contributes evidence on DTI and BMI from an underreported regional context.

title: Turning unknowns into value: How digital organizational ambidexterity drives digital innovation value creation under risk and uncertainty
HR analytics adoption and managerial decision-making style: The mediating role of human–AI interaction and the moderating role of attitude toward AI
Evaluating advantages and disadvantages of twin avatar-based management: A multicriteria framework for assessing organizational impacts
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital technologies are reshaping managerial decision-making by enabling new forms of interaction, simulation and action in increasingly immersive virtual environments. Among these technologies, Twin Avatars (TAs) ( i.e. , Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled digital representations of real individuals) are emerging as a potentially disruptive managerial tool with implications for organizational design, leadership and the future of work. By enabling enhanced digital presence, real-time interaction and scenario exploration, TAs can support faster and more adaptive decision-making in complex environments. Despite their growing relevance, research on the managerial implications of TA-based management remains limited. This study develops an analytic system to identify, structure and analyze key advantages and disadvantages associated with TA-based management. Adopting a constructivist perspective, the research combines the Nominal Group Technique (NGT) and DEcision MAking Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) under a neutrosophic logic framework, allowing for the explicit treatment of uncertainty and causal interdependencies among relevant factors. The analytic system was developed through facilitated expert sessions and subsequently consolidated by an independent expert. The results identify influential advantages and disadvantages of TA-based management and reveal the perceived causal relationships among them. The study advances understanding of how agentic AI-enabled technologies may influence organizational decision-making and provides a structured basis for evaluating the organizational implications of TA-based management.

Riding out uncertainty: Tech trade resilience across the US, China, and the European economies
abstract: Technology trade is highly exposed to uncertainty because it combines specialisation, cross-border production networks, and long investment horizons. This article examines how operational supply-chain pressure and trade-policy uncertainty are associated with technology-trade resilience across the US, China and selected European economies, conditional on countries’ lagged intermediate-goods trade exposure. We conceptualize technology-trade resilience in a bounded, trade-based sense as an observable dual-margin outcome reflected in the export-to-import ratio, capturing short-run trade-flow adjustment, and revealed comparative advantage, capturing structural export specialisation. The results reveal no uniform EI-RCA pattern across operational supply-chain pressure and trade-policy uncertainty. Operational supply-chain pressure is associated mainly with export-import adjustment, while changes in specialisation are selective. Trade-policy uncertainty is associated with more polarised sectoral outcomes, combining flow deterioration, specialisation vulnerability, and selective positive adjustment. Semiconductors and related electronic components display a distinctive positive response profile across the two resilience margins, although statistical precision varies across the two indicators and specifications. The findings show that technology-trade resilience cannot be inferred from trade balances alone and that product groups are internally heterogeneous and vary in their vulnerability and resilience.

Understanding students’ Generative AI use in higher education: A SEM-ANN analysis of AI attributes, behavioral reasons, and perceived learning performance
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools can support personalized educational experiences. However, limited understanding remains of how AI-specific human-like attributes and behavioral reasoning mechanisms jointly relate to students’ attitudes, self-reported Generative AI use, and perceived learning performance. To address this gap, this research integrates Behavioral Reasoning Theory (BRT) with key AI characteristics (perceived anthropomorphism, animacy, and intelligence) to examine students’ attitudes towards Generative AI and their association with perceived learning performance. Data were collected from 395 students who reported using Generative AI tools for academic activities. The study examined Generative AI broadly rather than a specific platform. Data were analyzed using a hybrid Structural Equation Modeling-Artificial Neural Network (SEM-ANN) approach. The results indicated that perceived anthropomorphism, animacy, intelligence, and reasons for adoption were positively associated with students’ attitudes, whereas reasons against adoption were not significantly associated with attitude. Self-reported Generative AI use was positively associated with students’ perceived learning performance. The ANN analysis ranked reasons for adoption as the most important predictor of students’ attitudes, with a normalized importance of 97.78%. The model explained 64.7% of the variance in students’ attitudes, 48% in self-reported Generative AI use, and 24.9% in perceived learning performance. This study contributes theoretically by extending conventional technology adoption research through integrating behavioral reasoning and AI-specific perception factors within the educational context.

title: How metaverse influencers shape electronic word-of-mouth: Credibility, attractiveness, and parasocial relationships across cultures and gender
abstract: Metaverse Influencers (MVIs) are technologically constructed social actors increasingly promoting tourism destinations. However, they continue to be viewed as uncannily or authentically fake, raising questions about whether followers perceive them as credible, form meaningful parasocial relationships with them, and intend to recommend the destinations they endorse. To address these gaps, this study integrated source credibility theory, parasocial relationship theory, and the similarity-attractiveness model and tested a framework linking source credibility and physical attractiveness to e-WOM intentions, with parasocial relationship as the mediator. Using a quantitative design across three cases (main effects/mediation; UK–USA–India; female–male), results showed that parasocial relationships increased e-WOM, and source credibility increased both parasocial relationships and e-WOM. Physical attractiveness did not directly increase e-WOM, but strengthened parasocial relationships, which fully mediated the attractiveness–e-WOM link; mediation was partial for credibility. Only one cross-country difference emerged (attractiveness to e-WOM was stronger in the USA), and one gender difference (attractiveness to parasocial relationship stronger for males). These findings show that the extent to which MVIs influence their followers is not only dependent upon the designed appearance of the MVI itself but also on whether followers perceive them as credible and develop parasocial relationships with them. The study enhances our knowledge of human relationships with synthetic social actors and provides insights into how MVIs should be created to responsibly promote tourism communications.

Technologies towards climate-neutral farming: Drivers of adoption and intentions across four European regions
abstract: Technological innovations are central to reducing agricultural greenhouse gas emissions. This paper investigates both the current uptake and intended future use of climate-mitigating technologies among farms in four European NUTS-1 regions: Wallonia (Belgium), Switzerland, Grand Est (France), and Ireland. Using survey data from 195 farms across diverse production systems, including arable-livestock and grass-based farming systems, we estimate Generalized Poisson (GP) regression models to assess technology uptake intensity. We also apply Multivariate Probit (MVP) models to identify technology-specific determinants and capture interdependencies among technology choices. The results suggest that structural characteristics such as land area, livestock units, and farmer age have limited practical relevance in explaining technology uptake. Instead, the strongest and most consistent associations are observed for behavioural traits, peer networks, and advisory exposure. Current uptake is primarily associated with technological knowledge, peer exposure, and productivity orientation. In contrast, intended future use is more closely associated with labour availability, business-oriented advice, formal training, and peer norms. The MVP results further indicate that current uptake is only partially coordinated, with patterns consistent with complementarity concentrated among specific technologies. Intended future use, by contrast, exhibits broader patterns of complementarity, suggesting that farmers more frequently envisage technologies as part of coordinated technology portfolios. Overall, these findings highlight the potential relevance of peer exposure, advisory and training systems, labour availability, and policy approaches supporting complementary technology portfolios for facilitating the transition towards climate-neutral farming systems.

abstract: Learning analytics models may offer timely support to enhance student’s preparedness and educator’s success metrics in their education career. This study models student performance using assessment data as a predictor for EAP7381 (a Mathematical and Computing Literacy course). To estimate the overall score (OS) for EAP7381, the proposed predictive model incorporates unique input combinations for models designated as (M01, M02, …, M09) that are drawn from five different types of assessments: computer skills (CS), problem solving (PS), class surveys/analysis (SA), revision exams (REs) and final exams (FTs). Using a 10-fold cross-validation approach on 466 student records, the support vector regression (SVR) model was benchmarked against extreme gradient boosting (XGB), K-nearest neighbour (KNN), and random forest (RF) models. The proposed SVR model demonstrated high degree of accuracy, yielding relatively low prediction errors that were between the estimated and actual OS values. In Model M02, the assessment PS that was administered between two and eight weeks demonstrated a strong correlation with OS, revealed through explainable artificial intelligence techniques: SHAP (SHapley Additive explanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) The results indicated that PS was a significant contributor to the performance of our proposed model. The LIME and SHAP results also demonstrated that the predictor variables based on FT and PS were the most influential indicators of the proposed learning analytics model. In the context of an applied educational setting, we therefore conclude that such assessments, when used to model students at-risk can be further explored for its potential utility to address student performance issues, failure s and attrition in order to develop necessary interventions. To support the educators in developing multidimensional pedagogical strategies, the proposed SVR model can be thus integrated into future commercially viable education technologies that offer data-driven guidance for enhancing the learning journey of our students.

Building vs Buying GenAI: A Techno-Economic Framework and Policy Reflections
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has led to measurable productivity gains and changes in work across sectors. For an organization that adopts GenAI, a basic decision is whether to develop its own system or purchase services from a vendor. The requirements differ from those of conventional software procurement. Specialized expertise and sensitive data are needed, while limited model transparency and continued retraining after deployment introduce further difficulties. Both capital and operating costs are substantial. Their economic justification depends on how extensively and consistently the system is used, and on whether demand is concentrated within particular functions or workflows. Earlier research provides useful insights, although a quantitative connection between costs and the value of productivity gains is still needed to determine the tipping point. We address this issue through a practical techno-economic framework that estimates the conditions under which building is economically preferable to buying. Productivity-based value estimates are combined with CAPEX and OPEX modelling. Total-cost-of-ownership principles are then applied within a Net Present Value analysis. The analysis indicates that use case intensity and scale, together with the deployment horizon, strongly affect the relevant-user break-even threshold. Greater utilization helps amortize capital costs and reduces this threshold. Marketing and computer programming reach the build threshold with comparatively few relevant users. Document search and summarization needs a moderate relevant-user base, whereas business productivity and customer support require wider or more intensive adoption. The framework adds explicit thresholds for each use case and user population to the qualitative guidance available in prior research. Scale is only part of the sourcing decision, as our findings also point to the role of specialization and governance. A specialized enterprise or department may have grounds for internal deployment. For a diversified organization comprising many small departments, purchasing generic tools or outsourcing specialized AI-enabled services may be reasonable. Shared AI infrastructure could alter these economics in the wider policy context. The framework can be used in enterprise strategy and in the evaluation of public investment in shared infrastructure. It can be extended to additional functions, hybrid sourcing configurations, dynamic pricing and quality outcomes, and to country- or sector-level calibration using local wages, productivity, energy prices, regulation, and firm demographics.

Seeing the Forest or the Tree: A Cross-country Comparison of Blame and Trust in Autonomous Vehicles after Accidents
abstract: Understanding cultural factors in public responses to autonomous vehicle (AV) incidents, including collisions and near-misses, is critical for the broader adoption of this technology, yet systematic cross-country comparisons are limited in the existing empirical literature. This paper presents three experiments in which judgments of blame and trust were collected from participants in the UK and Japan after viewing text and image-based vignettes (Experiment 1a and 1b) or watching video clips of driving scenarios (Experiment 2) featuring AVs or human drivers performing manoeuvres in traffic environments that ultimately led to collisions or near-misses. The findings reveal broadly similar baseline attitudes toward AVs but notable discrepancies between the two countries in post-incident judgments of blame: participants in Japan distributed blame more evenly across involved parties and scenarios, whereas greater variability in blame judgments was observed among UK participants. Indicative evidence was obtained that blame ratings in the UK were more affected by the perceived capability of AVs versus human drivers in a specific context compared to Japan. Possible causes for these discrepancies are discussed within the framework of cultural values and cognitive attributional styles. The findings lay empirical, methodological and theoretical foundations for future cross-cultural studies with implications for policymaking, legislation and the design of AV technology for multi-agent societies on a global scale.

An Immigrant Advantage in ChatGPT Adoption? Decomposing Nativity Gaps in Awareness, Use, and Perceived Helpfulness
abstract: A growing body of research has documented demographic disparities in generative AI adoption by age, education, income, and race/ethnicity, but whether adoption differs by immigration status remains unknown. Using data from the Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel (N=9,151), this study applied Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition to estimate the nativity gap in first-level AI adoption (ChatGPT awareness, ChatGPT ever use) and second-level AI adoption (specific use cases of entertainment, learning, and work tasks), and to determine how much of any observed difference is attributable to group characteristics versus differences in how those characteristics relate to outcomes. Findings show that foreign-born adults had higher rates of ChatGPT awareness (77.0% vs. 69.4%) and ChatGPT use (43.4% vs. 32.7%) after adjusting for age and gender. Among ChatGPT users, foreign-born adults were significantly more likely to use ChatGPT for learning (34.9% vs. 22.5%, p < .001). Age, education, race/ethnicity, and digital access were the primary contributors to the explained gap, though the relative importance of each factor varied across outcomes. For first-level adoption (ChatGPT awareness), sociodemographic differences accounted for 63% of the 9.9 percentage-point gap, with a significant unexplained component remaining (3.6 pp, adjusted p = .013) after FDR correction. For second-level adoption (ChatGPT use for learning), race/ethnicity alone accounted for nearly 80% of the explained gap. Recent immigrants (0-10 years in the U.S.) showed the highest ChatGPT engagement at the second level of adoption, and Spanish-language respondents reported lower first-level adoption of awareness (58.9% vs. 70.7%, p < .001) after adjusting for age and gender. These findings indicate that immigrant disadvantage in technology adoption does not extend to ChatGPT, and that language access and purpose of use are additional dimensions of AI inequality beyond nativity alone.
